title: The RBI Just Held Rates for the Third Straight Meeting. It Is Betting the War Will End Before Inflation Arrives.
excerpt: Governor Malhotra chose dollar incentives over a rate hike to defend the rupee. The inflation forecast rose to 5.1 per cent. The growth forecast fell to 6.6 per cent.
body:
The Reserve Bank of India held its benchmark repo rate steady at 5.25 per cent on Friday, the third consecutive meeting without a change, as Governor Sanjay Malhotra opted to wait out the Iran war's fallout rather than defend the rupee with costlier credit.

The decision was unanimous. All six members of the Monetary Policy Committee voted to hold, and to keep the policy stance at "neutral" — technically leaving the door open to move in either direction, though the inflation numbers are now pointing firmly upward.

## The Numbers That Changed

The RBI revised its inflation forecast for the current fiscal year to 5.1 per cent, up sharply from 4.6 per cent projected in April. The central bank expects price pressures to peak in the October-December quarter at 5.9 per cent, driven by crude oil prices, commercial LPG costs, and pass-through effects from elevated freight and insurance charges.

The GDP growth forecast was trimmed to 6.6 per cent from 6.9 per cent. Quarter by quarter, the picture is uneven: 6.6 per cent in Q1, a dip to 6.3 per cent in Q2, a recovery to 6.5 per cent in Q3, and 6.8 per cent in Q4.

"Although risks of higher inflation have amplified, the MPC felt it would be prudent to wait for greater clarity to emerge," Malhotra said. The phrasing was deliberate — an acknowledgement that the war in West Asia has made forecasting unusually difficult.

## The Rupee Defence Package

Instead of raising rates, the RBI chose to defend the rupee through capital account measures designed to pull dollars into India without tightening domestic liquidity.

The government scrapped capital gains tax on interest income earned by foreign portfolio investors on government securities — a direct incentive for overseas bond buyers. The RBI expanded the list of bonds eligible under the Fully Accessible Route, which allows unlimited foreign investment. And it sweetened the terms on dollar deposit schemes for non-resident Indians, the FCNR(B) facility, to encourage the diaspora to park more dollars in Indian banks. Public sector undertakings were also incentivised to tap external commercial borrowings for a limited period.

The rupee strengthened 0.6 per cent to 95.24 against the dollar after the announcement. The benchmark 10-year bond yield fell to 6.95 per cent.

## Why Not Hike?

Several emerging markets — Indonesia, the Philippines, Sri Lanka — have already raised rates in recent weeks to defend their currencies. India chose not to follow.

The reasoning is straightforward. Headline CPI inflation remains below the 4 per cent target, at 3.5 per cent in April, even as the forward projections climb. The inflation India is facing is supply-driven — crude oil, shipping costs, disrupted trade routes — not demand-driven. Raising rates would slow an economy already absorbing a terms-of-trade shock without addressing the underlying cause.

"A rate-led defence of the currency would have been an imprecise instrument at this juncture," said Vikram Chhabra, senior economist at 360 ONE Asset. "The RBI addressed the root issue — capital flows — rather than using the blunt tool of higher rates."

## What It Means for NRIs

The FCNR(B) sweetener is the most immediately relevant measure for the Indian diaspora. By raising the ceiling on interest rates that banks can offer on foreign currency deposits, the RBI is effectively competing for NRI dollars — money that would otherwise sit in American or British bank accounts earning lower yields.

The capital gains tax exemption on government bonds is aimed at institutional investors, but it could indirectly benefit NRIs holding Indian debt through mutual funds. Tax-exempt bond gains could attract more foreign capital, support the rupee, lower yields and improve broader investor sentiment.

The bigger question is whether these measures will be enough. The rupee has fallen nearly 5 per cent since the Iran war began in February, and record foreign portfolio outflows show that global investors are pulling money out of India, not putting it in. The RBI's forex reserves, while still substantial, have been depleted by months of intervention.

## What Comes Next

The next MPC meeting is in August. By then, the monsoon will have arrived — or failed to arrive adequately — and the trajectory of crude oil prices should be clearer. If inflation breaches 5.5 per cent and the rupee continues to weaken, the pressure for a rate hike will become difficult to resist.

Across the region, policymakers are already moving. South Korea has signalled a turn is imminent. The RBI is betting that the war will wind down, the strait will reopen, and the price shock will prove temporary. It is a bet on time — and time, in this conflict, has been the one thing in shortest supply.

*Sources: Reserve Bank of India policy statement, Reuters, The Hindu BusinessLine, LiveMint*
